items.en: Today, we release LFM2.5-24B-A2B, a 24B-parameter reasoning model with just 2B active parameters, built for fast, private agents on-device. It is the largest and final model in the LFM2.5 family, which now spans two orders of magnitude: from LFM2.5-230M to LFM2.5-24B-A2B.

LFM2.5-24B-A2B is competitive with Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, a model with ~50% more total and active parameters, on five of eight agentic and tool-use benchmarks, scoring 48.09 on LiveClaw versus 38.19 and 27.69 on AutomationBench versus 8.72. Because only 2B parameters are active per token, it runs up to 1.7× faster than comparable MoEs on-device, with 184 tokens/s on an Apple M5 Max and up to 21K output tokens/s on a single NVIDIA B300 GPU.

The base (LFM2.5-24B-A2B-Base) and post-trained (LFM2.5-24B-A2B) models are open-weight and available today on Hugging Face and our Playground. Check out our docs on how to run and fine-tune it locally.

LFM2.5-24B-A2B builds on our previous LFM2-24B-A2B release, with an expanded vocabulary and context window, scaled-up pretraining, and large-scale reinforcement learning. Unlike its predecessor, LFM2.5-24B-A2B is a reasoning-only model that produces an explicit chain of thought before its final answer. We adopted this strategy to leverage its high decode speed and improve answer quality.

Architecture. It keeps the 40 layers, 64 experts per MoE block with top-4 routing, and the same hybrid of gated short convolutions and GQA. The two architectural changes are the context window extension from 32,768 to 131,072 tokens, and the in-place tokenizer expansion, which doubles the vocabulary from 65K to 128K tokens for better non-Latin tokenization.
Pre-training was scaled up from 17T tokens to 33T tokens.

Mid-training has two phases. The first runs 2T tokens at 32K context on curated, higher-quality data weighted toward reasoning, math, code, instruction following, and multilingual text. The second runs 300B tokens at 131K context, weighted toward long context data. Tool calls and multi-turn trajectories appear throughout both phases to prepare the model for agentic workloads.

During teacher specialization, LFM2.5-24B-A2B exhibited well-known reward-hacking behaviors: searching for the final answer in a repository's git history or on platforms like GitHub, PyPI, and Hugging Face. More surprisingly, it even figured out it was in a sandbox, as shown in the examples below.

This behavior looks emergent but might be explained by training data containing similar patterns. We tightened our sandboxes in response, and all reported results below come from sealed evaluation environments.

We evaluated LFM2.5-24B-A2B across 16 benchmarks covering tool use and agentic workflows, knowledge, instruction following, math, and coding. Despite being the smallest model in total and active number of parameters, it is competitive with, and often outperforms, larger MoEs with ~50% more total and active parameters, such as Qwen3.6-35B-A3B.

LFM2.5-24B-A2B leads or matches the competition on five of the eight tool-use and agentic benchmarks (AutomationBench, BFCLv4, ToolSandbox, LiveClaw, and τ³-Bench Banking), with its widest margin on AutomationBench, where it scores more than three times the next-best model. It also leads on all three instruction-following benchmarks. Larger models keep an edge on knowledge-heavy benchmarks like GPQA Diamond, HLE, and AA-Omniscience, and on coding benchmarks like SWE-Bench Verified (OpenCode) and SciCode.

The results make LFM2.5-24B-A2B an ideal foundation for agents that need to reason, call tools, and run reliably on your device. For knowledge-heavy workloads, we recommend pairing LFM2.5-24B-A2B with retrieval or web search, which plays to its tool-calling strength.
LFM2.5-24B-A2B ships with day-one support across the inference ecosystem:
- llama.cpp — GGUF checkpoints for efficient edge inference
- MLX — Optimized inference for Apple Silicon
- vLLM — GPU-accelerated serving for production throughput
- SGLang — High-performance GPU serving framework
- ONNX — Cross-platform inference across diverse accelerators
All runs were collected on Pipette, the same benchmarking infrastructure behind Liquid AI's public device performance data.

Edge inference. Due to the efficient LFM2 architecture, LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest of the compared MoEs at reading in prompts and generating answers. It decodes 184 tokens/s on an Apple M5 Max and 114 tokens/s on an AMD Ryzen AI Max+ 395, up to 1.7x faster than the next-best model, while using the least memory.

GPU inference. To demonstrate the competitiveness of LFM architecture we compare the GPU inference throughput to other similarly sized MoE models. We measure GPU throughput (total output tokens / wall time) on a single NVIDIA B300 GPU using a sustained-load setting: at each concurrency level, we continuously maintain the target number of in-flight requests, replacing each completed request immediately.

We benchmark each model with SGLang 0.5.22, 1,024 input tokens, up to 256 output tokens, in BF16. LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest model in its size class, reaching over 21K output tokens per second at high concurrency.

LFM2.5-24B-A2B’s size, speed, and capabilities make it a great choice for agents that run continuously on your own hardware. In the demo below, we run it inside Hermes Agent on an M5 Max MacBook Pro, where it plans, calls tools, and works through a real task entirely on-device, without any cloud API calls.

The point of the demo is not the individual tools. It is that the tool-dispatch loop feels interactive on consumer hardware: ask, propose, confirm, run, repeat, all in well under a second per dispatch, with full audit trails and your data never leaving the device. Check out our local agent guide for how to serve the model locally and connect it with the agent harness of your choice.
Start building today with LFM2.5-24B-A2B, available on Hugging Face.

Over the past two days, 20 startups have been pitching on stage at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026, presenting live demos and answering tough questions from our expert judges. Now it’s time to unveil the five companies that will be competing in the Startup Battlefield finals.

This year’s Battlefield spanned four categories — space and physical AI, energy and manufacturing, health tech and life sciences, and enterprise and security — and our finalists are working on everything from miniature human organs to fighting scams to computing in space.

The finals will kick off tomorrow (Thursday) at 11:30 am Pacific — you can watch them on stage at Disrupt or on the livestream here. The founders will be presenting for another panel of expert judges who will pick the winner; that winner gets to take home the Startup Battlefield Cup and $100,000, equity-free.

Apate deploys thousands of AI agents that masquerade as innocent victims. The agents can answer scam calls, respond to shady messages and emails, follow phishing links, and join social media groups to bait fraudsters. They pretend to be people of all stripes, with different ages, genders, and accents, speaking various languages as they try to keep scammers engaged long enough to learn something useful.

Flox Intelligence has built a wildlife-deterrent system that works differently than the sirens, lights, fences, falcons, and culling traditionally used to keep animals away. Instead, it uses edge devices with perception systems trained on wildlife behavior. A motion sensor wakes the device when it detects movement, triggering a camera that uses on-device models to identify nearby animals. The device then emits a species-appropriate sound to scare them away.

Intero Biosystems is developing human intestinal organoids — lab-grown tissue that mimics the gut, as another way to study how drugs and other compounds might affect the human body before they are tested in people. Its organoids differ from simpler models that replicate only part of the gut. They contain multiple cell and tissue types found in the human intestine, which the company believes makes them a more human-relevant model for testing drugs and other compounds.

Industrial Next builds AI-driven, self-contained robotic stations powered by proprietary foundation models that connect vision, task context, and motion. The company says this lets a production line be retooled in minutes rather than weeks, without traditional programming. The goal is to let manufacturers automate complex and delicate tasks that traditionally require human labor. In fact, some of the startup’s workstations are already used in making one of the world’s most popular smartphones.

Satlyt is building software designed to allow many satellites to share the work of large computing jobs in space. The startup has already flown its software on two demonstration missions, with an initial focus on finding operational efficiencies for spacecraft. Those spacecraft typically depend on flight controllers on the ground to solve any problems that arise, with communication, so using AI to make decisions on the spacecraft can mean real savings. The next goal: to show that it can create a shared computing cloud between two satellites.
The US military’s race to make fake blood

In February 2007, a US military helicopter carrying blood to a field hospital was shot down in Iraq, killing all seven crew members. The mission was a reminder of the risks of transporting blood, which has a limited shelf life and is often in short supply.

Now, a $73 million DARPA effort aims to create shelf-stable versions of plasma, platelets, and red blood cells. The idea is to develop dried blood products that can be stored for long periods and deployed quickly on the battlefield.

The project aims to have bags of dried blood products deployed in the field by 2029. But getting it all done will be tough, and researchers still have major questions about the safety and effectiveness of synthetic alternatives.
10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch: WeLion New Energy and its semi-solid-state batteries

WeLion New Energy is on a quest to make safer, better batteries. The Chinese company’s liquid-solid hybrid cells aim to pack more power into electric cars, boats and drones, potentially improving safety and offering greater energy density than lithium-ion batteries.

In 2023, WeLion released a battery pack with EV-maker Nio that offered a range of over 1,000 kilometers. Now, the company is developing batteries with even higher energy density. But scaling up production and competing on cost remain major challenges.

Is the Pentagon allowed to surveil Americans with AI?

The ongoing public feud between the Department of Defense and the AI company Anthropic has raised a deep and still unanswered question: Does the law actually allow the US government to conduct mass surveillance on Americans?

Surprisingly, the answer is not straightforward. More than a decade after Edward Snowden exposed the NSA’s collection of bulk metadata from the phones of Americans, the US is still navigating a gap between what ordinary people think and what the law allows.
Today, the legal complexity has a new edge: AI is supercharging surveillance—and our laws haven’t caught up. Here’s how the Pentagon’s use of AI has exposed legal gray areas.

Hey, so, don’t rip down Rachel Chinouriri’s posters promoting her new album I Think I Spoke Too Soon, just so you can take pictures with Adéla’s “The Baddest Bitches Are in London” posters underneath them, okay? It’s rude to Chinouriri, a London-based pop artist who is just out here trying to make a living — plus Adéla, the singer behind “Nicole Kidman,” has now made it clear that she does not sanction this kind of fan behavior. “It’s [already] hard enough to make sure ur art gets out there & is heard… ESPECIALLY as a Black woman,” she wrote on Instagram on Tuesday.

In a since deleted video posted a few weeks ago, an Adéla fan showed herself ripping down Chinouriri’s posters with the caption, “That one time I tore down the Rachel Chinouriri poster to take pics w the Adela one but left Tyla’s one up cos she tanked.” Chinouriri herself responded on X, writing, “Hey so this isn’t okay.” She added that it’s tough enough for Black pop artists to get exposure, so ripping her poster down “is just quite mean and makes me pretty sad right now :(.” She also uploaded a response video to TikTok, telling the poster-ripper, “I also feel sad for you that that’s the attention that you’re enjoying.”

Adéla, who says she’s been on a social media hiatus, caught wind of the incident on Tuesday, when she condemned the fan behavior in an Instagram story. “Came across this way too late but u guys this is so fucking ass,” she wrote in the story. “Please don’t do this. Don’t take ppl’s posters down. Promotion costs money, Rachel’s posters cost money, they deserve to be up and seen.” In a follow up post, Adéla made sure to plug Chinouriri’s album, adding, “Anyways… I Think I Spoke Too Soon is out tomorrow!!! PRE-SAVEEE.”
If either of these two are ever considering a remix album… I have an idea for who their first collaborator could be.

There’s a tipsy sense of inversion in the title of Layla Khoshnoudi’s I’m Not Even Half that slowly seeps throughout the play, like the gradual spreading of dye in water. The phrasing suggests an empty-glass perspective, but Khoshnoudi carefully sets up the moment in which her character, known only as “S,” reminds us where she’s really looking from. “Where did this weakness come from? I should be strong like them,” she says, berating herself for what she feels as cowardice as she watches women protesting in the streets of Iran through the portal of her phone. “I’m Iranian. Full! Both sides. I’m not even half.”

S is a Brooklynite in 2022, hooked to her phone as the uprising in response to the murder of Mahsa Amini unfolds thousands of miles away and a few inches from her face. Earlier in the play, in her distraction, she stepped off the curb near Herbert Von King Park and a reversing car knocked her flat. As inciting incidents go, it’s a literal bash on the head, and Khoshnoudi uses it both to throw S into a tailspin and to wake her up. A smart, sad, self-laceratingly funny solo show in the tradition of Fleabag, I’m Not Even Half also brings to mind a more PG-rated lost heroine: After her bonk, S becomes an Alice down the rabbit hole of her own addictions and shames. She badly needs a perspective shift, a tumble head over heels, to show her just how clouded her own vision has been.

It’s also Emmie Finckel’s set — spare and ominously lit by Cheyenne Sykes, with its own portal opening cut out of the shadowed scrim back wall — that suggests falling down some murky spiraling tunnel. As she tells us her story, S navigates a variety of workaday New York settings — sidewalks and smoke shops, an ambulance, an Uber, a hospital, an apartment. The most exotic might be the CAT-scan machine where she sings a noodling, possibly concussed ode to her cooler-than-thou friend, Julianne, who surprises her by actually showing up after S texts her a bloodied duck-lips selfie. But Sykes, Finckel, and director Machel Ross intentionally and effectively blur the edges of all these environments. S mostly teeters from one dim pool of light to the next, as smears of luminous color appear and evanesce behind the set’s permeable backdrop, stoplights in the rain. It feels eerily empty, digital, ephemeral — as if S landed not on the asphalt of Marcy Avenue but inside the very phone that caused her injury. It’s a subtly impressive feat that Khoshnoudi gets us to laugh as much as she does from within such a container. This isn’t a space for comedy. It is, objectively, a bit nightmarish.

But S is determined to equivocate (and vape) away the shadows for as long as she can. Yes, what she’s seeing on social media is horrific, but comparatively, she’s, like, so completely fine, right? “Now we’re all familiar with this torturous phenomenon of being able to watch something terrible happen somewhere that you’re not,” she tells us dryly. “The feeling of being very, very close to something but not under direct threat by it — which, I’m not complaining: I can barely handle Literally Anything. I don’t want to be under direct threat!” The truth is that, as she tries to help “raise awareness with my posting,” she’s at least as fraught, if not more so, over the fact that an artsy guy called Harry isn’t texting her back. They’re on-again, off-again, and S talks about him like an alcoholic who insists she can quit any time. He’s a “crazy beast,” a “full Technicolor experience”; “the world is visibly less bright in his physical absence”; plus “like, he challenges me.”

The flags couldn’t be redder, and Khoshnoudi nimbly sketches out the circuitous emotional paths S takes to avoid seeing them until such evasion suddenly and brutally becomes impossible. The violence men inflict on women — perpetually, ruthlessly, everywhere, with or without the pretext of religion or “morality” — sits at the heart of I’m Not Even Half like a creature lurking at the center of a maze. Eventually, S will have to confront it without the distance of pixels, miles, or irony: The threat has always been more direct than she’s let herself admit.

The kind of mass upheaval that S is witnessing in her country of ancestry — the kind that makes her own life seem limp and little compared with its atrocities and its heroism — is right outside the boarded-up windows for the couple at the center of Delirium. But here, wherever here is, it’s clear that righteous protest is hardly the driving force behind the screams and the bombs, the sirens and building raids. Freely adapted by the director Igor Golyak from Ionesco’s 1963 play Délire à deux (usually titled in English Frenzy for Two, or More), Delirium takes place in a world of morbid foregone conclusions. The monsters are in power and the purges are taking place. The war is eternal — it may calm down for a while but it always restarts, its sides indiscernible and its cause irrelevant, and every time you look, another neighbor has been taken away.

No wonder its particular brand of dark absurdism — a mad dance in the face of a madder world — felt right to Golyak now. In the past I have found his work visually ingenious but heavy-handed, a popcorn machine of images that add vitality without always mitigating his tendency to make a big, blunt point early and often. That phenomenon is still at play in Delirium, but in Ionesco — and especially in the show’s power pair of actors, the Russian expats and brilliant clowns Andrey Burkovskiy and Chulpan Khamatova — Golyak has found means and material that suit his inclinations. The play is a series of games all hung on the hook of a deadly premise: What do you do with your time when you’re trapped, when the world is ending outside, when you have nothing but each other and time and who knows how much of it?

At the Irondale space in Fort Greene, on a dust-covered set (by Jan Pappelbaum and Cecilia Xuetong Feng) of exposed scaffolding and corrugated iron, Khamatova and Burkovskiy play two nameless lovers who spend their days in a whirl of slapstick and inane bickering. She says a snail and a turtle are the same animal; he disagrees. He bounces on a stack of mattresses that she’s sandwiched inside; she locks him in an imaginary bathroom; whenever they need someone to back them up in their frequent arguments, they each appeal passionately to their only friend, a large (real) goldfish bobbing stoically in a tank at the center of their destroyed room. Arguing is one of their primary forms of play, and play is all they have. Every so often an alarm will sound and they’ll freeze like hunted animals — or worse, something will explode outside and more dust, or worse, will fall from the crumbling ceiling. In Sasha Ageeva’s wonderful costumes, the pair look like zombified wedding guests, his tuxedo and frilly purple boutonnière and her blonde wig and sparkly dress caked in weeks (months, years?) of grime. It seems that one day, long ago, in a different world, they opened the door to go out to dinner together, or perhaps to the opera, and a bomb exploded on their doorstep. Like Looney Tunes characters, singed yet somehow alive, they shut the door and never opened it again.

Now their lives are a haunted, claustrophobic cartoon, and Golyak revels in its theatrical opportunities. His collaboration with sound designer Denis Zabiyaka is particularly compelling, as the couple futz with an ancient radio that’s periodically brought to life by their shenanigans, or when Burkovskiy, himself a kind of human record player, smacks his own head to start a tune playing in the space. It’s the kind of galvanic seeming-chaos that’s choreographed down to the microbeat, and there’s real satisfaction in watching Golyak’s actors, both figure skaters in previous lives, execute its loops and axels.

“Are you hurt?” she asks him desperately after one of the explosions outside rocks their bizarre little hideaway. He shakes his head and asks her the same: “Are you hurt?” It’s a moment of tenderness that adds ballast to the gymnastic clownery, as well as a crucial hint that these two survivors — and perhaps this is their tragedy — haven’t yet entirely lost their minds. They still care for each other, and for that expressionless fish, whose tank they cover with a busted door whenever they think the ceiling might rain plaster. That care is the sorrowful heartbeat of Delirium. It’s what the surrounding violence is trying to stamp out, and it’s what commits us to following when one of these acrobats of make-believe implores the other, “Go see if another existence exists.”
I’m Not Even Half is at the Bushwick Starr through October 31.
Delirium is at the Space at Irondale through November 7.

At first, Maple was by my side. Kirsten Gillibrand’s Labradoodle pressed herself against my legs, happily accepting scratches and offering up a stuffed animal she hoped I would tug from her mouth (I obliged). New York’s junior senator, her once-blonde hair now closer to the white of Maple’s coat, then sat down across from me in her office, ready to explain how cryptocurrency had become one of her most prominent legislative priorities.

It was not an obvious place for her to end up. Two decades ago, Gillibrand won election to the House as a right-leaning Democrat from a conservative upstate district. After her appointment to Hillary Clinton’s vacated Senate seat three years later, she moved sharply left, emerging as a leading voice against sexual assault in the military and on college campuses. At the height of the Me Too movement, she led the charge in calling for Senator Al Franken to resign, then ran for president in 2019 as a staunch progressive, describing some of her former positions as moral failings and warning against “circles and systems of power” sustained by “corruption and greed.” Today, she is the Democratic Party’s leading champion of an industry notorious for fraud, spectacular collapses, and scams — and the eye-watering sums it spends to win the favor of politicians in both parties.

Crypto appeared on Gillibrand’s radar not long after her presidential campaign fizzled out. She said she first heard about it from constituents and financial regulators, then in hearings about cybercrime and illicit finance. “In the early stages, nobody knew anything about it. I didn’t know anything about it. So I started reading some books and listening to podcasts and trying to understand what the industry was about,” she told me.

The more she learned, she said, the more frustrated she became that lawmakers seemed content to leave it alone. “What I was seeing from Congress is that they were too unwilling and unable to learn about a new industry and actually do the basic regulation,” she added. Before running for Congress, Gillibrand spent 15 years as a securities lawyer. “I was very knowledgeable about credit default swaps when most of my colleagues didn’t even know what a credit default swap was,” she explained. “Complex commercial issues that need to be regulated are something I’m just very familiar with, and it’s not scary for me.”

In 2025, Gillibrand was the lead Democratic sponsor of the GENIUS Act, which laid down federal rules for stablecoins, or tokens designed to avoid the wild price swings of cryptocurrencies by pegging them to the U.S. dollar. Reporting at the time described her roaming the Senate floor with a binder, buttonholing skeptical Democrats, listening to their problems with the bill, and carrying their proposed changes back to Republican negotiators. Eighteen Senate Democrats, almost all of them recipients of crypto largesse, joined Republicans to pass the bill.

This year, she played much the same role for the CLARITY Act, the crypto industry’s great unfinished legislative project, pressing fellow Democrats for their votes. The sweeping bill would have moved much of digital-asset trading out of the Securities and Exchange Commission’s securities-law regime and into a new framework overseen by the chronically underfunded and much weaker Commodity Futures Trading Commission. The previous SEC had sued major trading platforms, including Coinbase, Kraken, and Binance, only for the suits to be dropped once Trump was sworn in for a second term. This was “why CLARITY was so existential for the industry,” according to Amanda Fischer, who served as chief of staff in the Biden SEC. The bill would have “codified and blessed their business structures and protected past conduct from future enforcement.”

It would also have made it easier for banks and other traditional financial firms to enter the crypto market, allowing them to trade, hold, lend against, and process payments in digital assets — an enormous step toward knitting the crypto industry into the traditional financial system. The bill appeared headed for passage until negotiations foundered over how to prevent elected officials from profiting from crypto, a newly urgent question given the Trump family’s budding crypto empire. When Republicans brought the bill to the floor without a bipartisan agreement on stronger ethics provisions, it became clear the bill would fail, and Gillibrand joined the rest of the Democratic caucus in voting “no.”

Gillibrand is not only one of crypto’s most important Democratic allies but also chair of the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, responsible for raising money for her colleagues. According to reporting by Punchbowl News, Gillibrand’s chief of staff, Jess Fassler, invoked his boss’s fundraising position while urging other Democratic aides to help advance the GENIUS Act, according to four aides present. Some took the remark as an implicit warning about the political consequences of crossing the industry. (Fassler denies making any threats.)

Gillibrand now finds herself in a crypto-related ethical morass that extends beyond her chief of staff’s remarks. Her 22-year-old son, Theo, is the head of a start-up backed in part by crypto investors — including one who donates to his mother and the DSCC — that is seeking regulatory approval to bring a crypto-native trading product into conventional financial markets. Her campaign coffers are stuffed with crypto money, while former aides have rotated between her office and the industry. When I mentioned that her former communications director had made crypto purchases a week before she announced her first stab at crypto regulation, Gillibrand said she had “no lens on that at all.” Her office, she said, tells employees “to be good people and serve the state of New York and help people every day.”
By then, Maple, who had spent the interview pressed against my legs, was barking at me.

When Gillibrand first became aware of crypto, she said, it looked to her like an answer to a problem she had spent years trying to solve: the roughly one in five New York households that are unbanked or underbanked. Her attempts to authorize banking through the post office were being blocked by Republicans who opposed it as more big government and unfair competition for local banks. “One of the use cases of crypto that was brought to me very early when I started meeting with stakeholders — they’re like, ‘This democratizes finance,’” she said. Eventually, she concluded, “I could then accomplish what I was trying to accomplish with postal banking by highly regulating an industry that’s making banking available to everybody who doesn’t have a bank account.”

In 2022, Gillibrand heard that Cynthia Lummis, a Republican senator from Wyoming, wanted to work on crypto regulation too. Lummis was an enthusiast as well as an investor: She had first bought bitcoin in 2013 and purchased an additional $50,001 to $100,000 worth in August 2021, a transaction she disclosed late under the STOCK Act — the transparency law Gillibrand herself had sponsored. Gillibrand approached her. “Why don’t we write the regulation?” she remembered asking. “Why don’t we do the rules of the road? Because this industry has so much corruption, so much grift, so much wild west.”

The same year, Gillibrand and Lummis introduced the Responsible Financial Innovation Act, which attempted to divide regulatory authority over crypto assets between the SEC and the CFTC. That September, Gillibrand also co-sponsored a bill handing oversight of crypto spot markets, where digital assets are bought and sold for immediate delivery, to the CFTC. This was the legislation Sam Bankman-Fried, who had donated to Gillibrand that June, was lobbying for so aggressively it became widely known as the “SBF bill.” When FTX collapsed months later, many Democrats rushed to distance themselves from Bankman-Fried and crypto generally. Gillibrand gave his donations to charity but drew the opposite lesson. For her, the spectacular failure of FTX was proof not that crypto should be kept at arm’s length but that Congress had waited too long to bring it under the umbrella of financial regulation.

Gillibrand’s answer to nearly every criticism of crypto is that it makes regulation only more urgent, not less. “Why would you allow a trillion-plus-dollar industry to go around allowing people to buy and sell shit and not regulate it?” she asked me. My suggestion that Congress might be better off refusing to legitimize the industry exasperated her. “It’s such an uneducated perspective,” she said. “It’s like saying ‘Don’t regulate the internet.’” Crypto was, of course, being monitored and targeted by the SEC, but Gillibrand contended that many crypto tokens function more like commodities, hence making the CFTC a more appropriate regulator — which is what the industry argues as well.

One of Gillibrand’s central rationales — that digital assets can bring the under- and unbanked into the financial system — has an obvious problem. Tonantzin Carmona, the director of economic policy at the Century Foundation who studies financial inclusion and cryptocurrency, noted that most ordinary consumers buy crypto through apps and exchanges that generally require a bank account or debit card. Crypto ATMs offer a cash work-around but can carry steep fees and have become fertile ground for scams.

The greater concern is what happens if Gillibrand succeeds in making crypto easier to use and more deeply embedded in ordinary finance. “In my opinion, the CLARITY Act was a financial crisis waiting to happen,” Lee Reiners, a former Federal Reserve Bank of New York official who teaches financial regulation at Duke University, told me. When FTX collapsed in 2022, the damage remained largely contained within crypto because digital assets still had relatively few connections to banks and traditional markets. CLARITY, Reiners argued, would have helped erase that separation: “Certainly, if CLARITY had passed, it would have supercharged the integration of crypto into the financial system.” At the same time, he said, the bill would have given the industry a “patina of regulation” — enough of a federal seal of approval to attract more customers and institutions without imposing the full set of rules that governs conventional securities firms. “The crypto industry wanted this bill to pass,” he said, “so they could point and say, ‘Look, we are regulated now. Come on in. The water’s warm and nice.’”

Corey Frayer, who served as a senior adviser to former Biden SEC chair Gary Gensler and worked on crypto-asset policy, argued that the entire theory behind CLARITY was misguided. “The securities laws are not only about the business you’re offering,” Frayer told me. “The securities laws are primarily about how you raise money for that business.” If a company raises money from investors by promising them profits, he explained, it must comply with securities laws, including disclosure requirements, whether it’s developing a conventional product or a cryptocurrency. To him, the industry’s argument for different rules amounted to companies insisting they shouldn’t have to follow those laws because — he waved his hands — “technology.” He pointed to Coinbase, which combines functions that conventional finance generally separates: exchange, custody, clearing, and brokerage and venture investing. For an industry that talks frequently about democratizing finance, Frayer said, “the crypto market is actually far less democratic. It is far more concentrated, more run by powerful, concentrated interests than even the admittedly broken traditional markets.”

Mark Hays, who specializes in cryptocurrency and financial technology for the nonprofits Americans for Financial Reform and Demand Progress, put it this way: “They just want to become your bank, your broker, and everything else under one roof — but without the same rules those entities have to agree to because we spent 100 years trying to keep them under regulatory check.”

Even bitcoin, widely regarded as the most decentralized and commodity-like cryptocurrency, is less so than its proponents claim, according to Hilary Allen, a professor at American University’s law school who specializes in financial regulation. “Bitcoin’s actually not particularly decentralized,” she told me, since only a handful of mining pools is responsible for producing the vast majority of new blocks on the bitcoin network.

The GENIUS Act, signed into law last year, created other potential hazards. The law requires stablecoin issuers to back their tokens one-for-one with assets including cash and short-term Treasury securities. To Allen, that could become a source of systemic risk if stablecoins grow large enough. A run on a major stablecoin would force its issuer to raise cash to meet redemptions, potentially by selling Treasuries. “If you dump a lot of Treasuries at one point,” Allen told me, “you’re going to cause haywire in the Treasuries market,” which underpins much of the global financial system. She also noted that stablecoins resemble money-market mutual funds, which the government has had to stabilize during previous crises.

Gillibrand makes the opposite case: Tying stablecoins to cash and Treasuries under federal supervision makes the market safer, not more dangerous. “You don’t reduce systemic risk by pretending a market doesn’t exist,” one of her aides told me.

Many of the fears about crypto ultimately depend on its becoming much bigger than it is today. “There’s all kinds of financial-stability implications, but they’re by and large premised on volume,” Allen said. “So if no one uses these things, then most of the risks are avoided.”
This is a point on which the two sides agree, sort of. Gillibrand told me what she expects to happen with crypto if she gets the CLARITY Act through in the future.
“Once it’s regulated,” she said, “people will be able to use it much more.”

The industry would naturally also like that to happen. And Gillibrand has benefited greatly from big crypto’s generosity. Donors to her 2024 reelection campaign included Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong; Ripple co-founder Chris Larsen and chief legal officer Stuart Alderoty; Electric Capital co-founders Avichal Garg and Curtis Spencer; Solana co-founder Raj Gokal; Digital Currency Group executive Mark Murphy; and Andreessen Horowitz co-founders Marc Andreessen and Ben Horowitz, along with their wives, Felicia Horowitz and Laura Arrillaga-Andreessen.

After Gillibrand’s election, the money kept coming. Contributors to her campaign or affiliated committees since then have included Coinbase president Emilie Choi and chief policy officer Faryar Shirzad; Paradigm co-founder Fred Ehrsam and managing partner Alana Palmedo; Ripple CEO Brad Garlinghouse; Andreessen Horowitz crypto partner Chris Dixon; Kraken chairman Jesse Powell and co-CEO David Ripley; and Tyler Winklevoss, the Gemini co-founder and major crypto donor who, with his brother, Cameron, personally lobbied Trump against his first nominee to chair the CFTC, Brian Quintenz, helping derail his nomination. Trump instead installed Mike Selig, a former lawyer for cryptocurrency firms and prediction markets.

In June, Gillibrand’s son Theo raised $30 million for a start-up called American Perpetuals Exchange Corporation. The fundraising round was led by Lux Capital — a shareholder of FTX before it collapsed — which valued the company at $300 million. One of Theo’s angel investors is Chris Larsen, the Ripple co-founder and Gillibrand donor. Although APEC is not a cryptocurrency exchange (it wants to offer perpetual futures on stocks and stock indexes, a type of highly leveraged derivative with no expiration date), the product came to prominence in crypto markets. These contracts provide no new capital to the companies whose shares they track. Instead, they offer traders another way to gamble on price swings, potentially magnifying losses and spreading them through the broader financial system — a familiar Wall Street arrangement in which the profits are private but the risks are everyone’s problem.

Theo himself is a product of the crypto world. Before graduating from Stanford, he interned at Andreessen Horowitz and completed a fellowship at Paradigm. In May 2025, while his mother was helping push GENIUS through the Senate, he co-authored an article in a Stanford newspaper founded by Peter Thiel urging Congress to pass the bill, without disclosing his obvious connection to its lead Democratic sponsor.

Theo Baker, a Stanford classmate of Theo Gillibrand’s and the author of a recent book about the university’s relationship with Silicon Valley, offers a perspective on how a 22-year-old with the right last name ends up running a $300 million crypto-inspired finance company. At Stanford, Baker said, a network of investors and scouts is on the lookout for teenagers who can be “quickly and heavily monetized.” APEC said Lux did not recruit Theo Gillibrand while he was at Stanford, but its success does depend heavily on a good relationship with regulators in Washington. The company has found open doors at Trump’s SEC and CFTC, the agencies that will determine whether and how its novel contracts can legally trade. Theo Gillibrand has said that CFTC officials were “very excited” by his proposals and that Trump’s financial regulators were more willing to listen than their predecessors had been.

A crypto ecosystem has developed around Senator Gillibrand’s office as well. Before joining Gillibrand’s staff and working on crypto legislation, Dorothy DeWitt worked at Coinbase, then ran a division of the CFTC. Andrew Siegel went from serving as general counsel at Galaxy, one of the country’s largest crypto firms, to a senior counsel job with Gillibrand. The revolving door is hardly unusual in Washington, but one case inside Gillibrand’s office raises a different question.

Senior congressional staff are required to file financial-disclosure statements if they earn above a certain threshold. When I pulled those of Evan Lukaske, Gillibrand’s former communications director and the aide handling her crypto messaging, they indicated he had bought between $1,001 and $15,000 of bitcoin on March 9, 2022, and the same amount of ether eight days later. A week later, Gillibrand announced she and Lummis were writing comprehensive crypto legislation. That bill — the first stab at what would eventually become known as CLARITY — specifically placed bitcoin and ether under CFTC commodity regulation, and Lukaske served as a spokesman defending it when it was unveiled that June. Lukaske did not respond to questions about what he knew when he made the trades or whether he was acting on nonpublic information.

Chris Swartz, senior counsel and deputy director of ethics at Democracy Defenders Fund and a former federal-government ethics official, stopped short of saying those trades establish wrongdoing. But, he said, Gillibrand’s staffers “should have known that purchasing crypto might create at least the appearance of impropriety.” Whether Lukaske’s purchases were “simply inadvisably timed trades or suggest use of nonpublic information for private gain is a question of fact that would have to be looked into,” Swartz said. Either way, “the timing raises serious concerns.”

I asked Gillibrand whether she had ever given her staff guidance about trading cryptocurrency. “No,” she said, “we don’t involve ourselves with our staff at all about what they own and what they have.”
Would she have a problem with staff members buying crypto while she was working on legislation that could benefit the industry?
“I could care less what they do with their money,” she said. “This is not a nanny state.”
It started as a supplement for athletes, and now scientists are investigating the benefits of creatine for more than just muscle.
According to preliminary evidence, this natural organic compound could have perks for many parts of the body and brain even without exercise.
That idea remains contentious; however, a new study among rats suggests that creatine is highly effective at protecting the brain from a disrupted gut.
The findings, published in Brain, Behavior, and Immunity, are limited to animal models, but researchers in Spain believe there are clinical implications.
In individuals with gut-brain inflammatory disorders, they argue, creatine could be an "excellent candidate" to preserve brain health.

"From a clinical perspective, creatine supplementation emerges as a powerful, complementary and preventive strategy," the research team concludes, led by neurophysiologists Alejandro Ruiz-Calero and Maria Ortego-Domínguez at the University of Seville in Spain.
"… it restores hippocampal creatine content, preserves neuronal integrity, and normalizes neuronal excitability by selectively targeting parameters disrupted by inflammation."
Last year, some of the same researchers found that creatine supplementation in rodents reduced gut inflammation and disease-related damage within the intestine.
Their new experiments show perks for the hippocampus, too, which is a crucial brain region involved in learning and memory.
When rats with gut inflammation took creatine daily, the supplement successfully restored creatine levels in their hippocampus.
It also reduced inflammation and damage to neurons in this region.
The results align with several preliminary studies linking creatine supplementation to improved brain health.
The brain is known to use a huge amount of the body's energy, and creatine plays an important role in maintaining our cellular energy balance.
For humans, a typical omnivorous diet involves about 1 to 2 grams of creatine a day. This natural organic compound is also made by the liver, the kidneys, and the pancreas.
Once produced or consumed, it is mostly stored within muscle, but creatine can also cross the blood-brain barrier and be taken up by neurons and other brain cells.
What it does once it is in the central nervous system is less clear.
This new research suggests that creatine supplements may impact the health and function of certain brain cells.
The rodents in experiments were modeled on a human condition called ulcerative colitis, which, together with Crohn's disease, is considered a chronic inflammatory bowel disease (IBD).
Ulcerative colitis causes the immune system to attack the intestinal lining, leading to open sores in the colon and rectum.
But its symptoms are not confined to the gut. They are also apparent in the brain.
When IBD flares up and is considered 'active', patients often report brain fog, and display memory loss, attention deficits, and declining executive functions.
In rats with colitis, previous studies have shown that the disease leads to greater inflammation in the hippocampus.
Now, researchers in Spain have extended those results and shown that gut inflammation in rats can also lead to damage and dysfunction within hippocampal neurons.
The good news, however, is that oral doses of creatine seem to help.
In experiments, some rats were given water containing one gram of creatine per kilogram of their body weight.
Then 10 days later, the scientists induced symptoms of colitis. The daily creatine dose continued for the rest of the experiment.
In rats that took creatine but didn't have colitis, researchers did not measure a significant change to creatine levels in the hippocampus.
But in rats with colitis, creatine improved several markers of healthy brain activity.
"The supplementation restored hippocampal creatine levels, preserved neuronal integrity, and normalized impaired excitability," the authors conclude.
Interestingly, the research team found that the benefits of creatine for male rats with colitis were more apparent than for females.
This is probably because in males, the brain damage associated with colitis seems to be worse than in the opposite sex.
The findings suggest that some inflammatory conditions may impact the male and female brain differently, and that creatine supplementation may help prevent some of these ramifications.

"Beyond colitis, reduced brain creatine content has been linked to systemic and central nervous system inflammatory disorders, including neurodegeneration, traumatic brain injury, and neuropsychiatric disease," the authors explain.
But much of the research on creatine and the brain remains in the preclinical stage, so it is unclear how effective this supplement might be in humans.
Initial findings among rodents suggest that not everyone will benefit in the same way.

Earlier this year, on the Health vs Hype podcast, Jason Mitchell, the chief medical officer at healthcare company Geisinger, said that recent results on creatine and brain health were intriguing but hardly definitive.
"We don't have the data to say, yeah, this is something you should be taking for your brain, but I don't want to discount that. There are some studies out there."
Researchers from Spain have now added another to the list.
The research has been published in Brain, Behavior, and Immunity.
The Air Force is looking to replace the three-decade-old radar warning system that protects the coastlines and borders of the United States and a few remote locations.
A Sept. 21 notice from the Air Force Life Cycle Management Center seeks sources for new technology to continue the Air Route Surveillance Radar-4’s mission and potentially improve its technology.
The notice’s details are classified, but AFLCMC updated the original notice Oct. 13, according to Sam.gov.

The number of radars needed to replace the 44-radar network and the price for those replacements has not yet been determined and will come via market research, Air Force Materiel Command spokesperson Mark Wyatt told Air & Space Forces Magazine.
There is also no development timeline publicly available, though responses to the sources sought notice are due by Oct. 21.
Wyatt said AFLCMC is requesting an instrumented range of 250 nautical miles, identical to the current ARSR-4.

ARSR-4 helps operators distinguish aircraft or potential missile threats from other radar “clutter,” which is more prevalent at lower altitudes. While historically the radar has been very effective at this task, newer additions to the cluttered landscape, namely wind farms, can distort the radar’s ability to “see” clearly.
“Wind farms are one of many sources of clutter that any solution would have to address,” Wyatt said. “The Air Force is not prescribing any technique to solve this long-standing challenge for radars.”
Interested industry parties can continue to pair their replacement option with the existing Monopulse Maintenance Surveillance Radar or replace that radar with another solution, Wyatt said.
The MMSR works with the ARSR-4 to “interrogate” aircraft transponders it detects by sending out coded radio frequency pulses that the transponder then responds to.
Using the monopulse method, the MMSR can determine an aircraft’s azimuth from a single pulse received from the transponder, instead of needing multiple hits when sweeping the area.
The MMSR is mounted on the ARSR-4, and they rotate together as they monitor the skies.
The Air Force purchased most of the existing 44 radars in the 1990s, upgrading the previous 1, 2, and 3 models that have monitored the skies since the late 1950s.

The Raytheon-built ARSR-1 entered service in 1958 and was first used to manage the exploding growth of civil aviation. It had a 170-200 nautical mile range. That early system used the Army/Navy/Fixed Radar Surveillance-20 and later variants of the AN/FPS-66. In the 1960s, Raytheon produced the ARSR-2, which improved maintenance and reliability factors. That radar was the AN/FPS-115.
Both the ARSR-1 and -2 ran on vacuum tubes.

Westinghouse Electric Corporation built the AN/FPS-130, the radar base of the ARSR-3, fielding it in the 1970s and extending detection ranges beyond 240 nautical miles; it was incorporated into joint military-civil air defense networks.

The ARSR-4, also built by Westinghouse and commissioned in the 1990s, was the first radar in the family to offer three-dimensional target tracking. That capability allows users to simultaneously measure a target’s range, azimuth, and altitude. The system also provided advanced look-down/clutter rejection capabilities for military operations.
Northrop Grumman acquired Westinghouse in 1996, rolling the company’s radar and electronic warfare programs into its Electronic Systems sector.

While the ARSR-4s monitor the perimeter of the country, Guam, and Guantanamo Bay, Cuba, for the U.S. interior, the FAA manages a network of Common Air Route Surveillance Radars. The CARSR has an estimated 200 nautical mile range.
The complete CARSR system replacement rollout concluded in 2015. The rollout maintained the legacy sites, towers, and mechanical controls while refitting the internal electronics of the radars.

One ARSR-4 location has a strategically vital area to protect: Watford City, N.D., is 165 miles from Minot Air Force Base, N.D., home of the 91st Missile Wing, and 263 miles from Malmstrom Air Force Base, Mont.—putting hundreds of ICBM silos in its range.
The ARSR-4 system is one piece of a larger detection system used to track incoming threats.

The Air Force and NORAD used the AN/FPS-117 and AN/Transportable Phased Array System-77, both of which serve as northern warning systems out to 250 nautical miles. These systems are specifically designed for extreme cold weather, such as in their locations in Alaska and northern Canada.

The Space Force operates the AN/Frequency Precision and Quantization-16 Perimeter Acquisition Radar Attack Characterization System, which tracks missiles and precision space objects out to about 2,000 miles. USSF also operates the AN/FPS-108 COBRA DANE to track missiles out to 2,000 miles and high-altitude space objects at 25,000 miles.
The Space Force’s 20th Space Surveillance Squadron at Elgin Air Force Base, Fla., operates the AN/FPS-85 Phased Array Radar, which can track objects beyond 22,000 miles.

NORAD is also currently building and deploying high-frequency systems to detect hypersonic missiles with over-the-horizon radar, modernizing the Northern Warning System and building a polar over-the-horizon radar network.

The Homeland Defense OTHR, which kicked off in 2022, is being funded by both the United States and Canada at an estimated $6-7 billion and $3.1 billion, respectively. Initial Operating Capability is slated for 2028-29, with Full Operational Capability targeted for 2031.
Canada’s Polar OTHR is expected to cost up to $3.5 billion and is a slice of the nation’s estimated $38.6 billion overhaul of its portion of NORAD.
The polar project is currently in the site procurement phase, with operational deployment planned for 2029 and FOC by 2033.
The U.S. Northern Warning System Modernization project “Crossbow” could cost up to $6 billion, and the system rollout is expected to last until 2028, with the project concluding in 2035.

The High-Altitude and Mobile Near-Space Surveillance Systems has a $4.2 billion contract ceiling and is currently in field testing and initial low-altitude deployments. It is expected to achieve full cloud-based command-and-control network integration by 2028.

Last November, NASA and its European partners launched the Sentinel-6B satellite to improve hurricane forecasts, help protect infrastructure, and benefit commercial industries, including shipping. The satellite now is flying 30 seconds behind its predecessor, Sentinel-6 Michael Freilich. Both satellites are providing precise sea level height measurements during what oceanographers expect to be a historic El Niño, a naturally occurring oceanic phenomenon in which warmer-than-usual Pacific waters shift global weather patterns.

The two satellites make up the Copernicus Sentinel-6/Jason-CS (Continuity of Service) mission, the latest in a series of ocean-observing radar altimetry missions that have been monitoring Earth’s changing seas continuously since the early 1990s.
The data each satellite is collecting will not only allow scientists to better understand this year’s El Niño but will also help them create more accurate hurricane predictions.

“This El Niño was a late-bloomer,” said Josh Willis, Sentinel-6B’s project scientist at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California. “It didn’t kick off until the middle of the year and is just now reaching a strength similar to what we’ve seen in the satellite record during significant El Niños in 1997 and 2015. We expect it to be big, and it’s already having big impacts.”

El Niños generally scramble weather patterns tied to rainfall and storms, including hurricanes. They also redistribute heat in the ocean, which affects sea level. Normally, Earth’s warmest ocean waters sit along the equator in the western Pacific. During El Niño, weakened winds, which usually blow westward along the equator, result in heat spreading east toward South America. The change in ocean heat shifts hurricane activity from the Atlantic to the Pacific Ocean.

On July 15, Sentinel-6B began delivering low-latency data to scientists that could be used for weather predictions. That data will take some time to work its way into the research models on which meteorologists and climate scientists rely, but when it does, those improved models could save lives.

Data from Sentinel-6 satellite missions feeds into hurricane tracking algorithms used by federal and state agencies. Those predictions can activate disaster response efforts, mobilizing resources ranging from sandbag placement to National Guard activation. They also can lead to evacuation orders that require quick but well-informed decisions about logistics at a local level. More severe events may require engaging larger organizations, such as the Federal Emergency Management Agency.

A tropical storm can take a week or more to become a hurricane and make its way to a coastline, but a hurricane can rapidly intensify in the 48 hours prior to landfall, leaving planners little time to prepare.

“Hurricanes have been known to speed up quickly at the last moment, so the window in which to decide what to do is short,” said Deirdre Byrne, an oceanographer and altimetry expert with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA). “The goal is to forecast how much and how rapidly intensification will happen so that officials can make the right calls.”
Byrne oversees one of the country’s most crucial hurricane forecasting algorithms, NOAA’s Satellite Ocean Heat Content Suite, which has been operating since 2012.

Each Sentinel-6 satellite measures ocean height, as well as the size of waves and marine wind speed, using a radar altimeter, which bounces thousands of radar pulses a second off the crests and troughs of waves. Ocean height varies from place to place and provides insight into the ocean’s heat content, since warm water expands. That, in turn, helps forecast how fast hurricanes will grow.

The satellites each carry a second instrument, called the Global Navigation Satellite System - Radio Occultation (GNSS-RO), which measures atmospheric properties, such as humidity, pressure, and temperature.

Among the measurements Sentinel-6 is gathering, Byrne is most anticipating the ocean height data, which she plans to begin incorporating into the current Satellite Ocean Heat Content Suite algorithm by the end of the year.
“In terms of data quality, the Sentinel-6 missions are unparalleled,” Byrne said.

Together, the missions are also extending a precise dataset deep into its fourth decade. This record of sea level observations traces back to the TOPEX/Poseidon mission, which launched in 1992, and continues through to the present day with Sentinel-6 Michael Freilich. Sentinel-6B will take over for its predecessor as the reference satellite for global sea level measurements later this year.

“The key is consistency, measuring the same way, every time,” said Severine Fournier, Sentinel-6B deputy project scientist, JPL. “That’s what lets us predict hurricanes, and, in turn, protect coastal communities and infrastructure.”
Sentinel-6 Michael Freilich, named after a former director of NASA’s Earth Science Division, is one of two satellites that compose the Copernicus Sentinel-6/Jason-CS mission.

Sentinel-6/Jason-CS, a part of the European Union’s Earth observation program called Copernicus, was jointly developed by ESA (European Space Agency), EUMETSAT (European Organisation for the Exploitation of Meteorological Satellites), NASA, and NOAA, with funding support from the European Commission and technical support on performance from the French space agency CNES (Centre National d’Études Spatiales). Spacecraft monitoring and control, as well as the processing of all the altimeter science data, is carried out by EUMETSAT on behalf of the European Union’s Copernicus Programme, with the support of all partner agencies.

NASA JPL, a division of Caltech in Pasadena, contributed three science instruments for each Sentinel-6 satellite: the Advanced Microwave Radiometer, the GNSS-RO, and the Laser Retroreflector Array. NASA also contributed launch services, ground systems supporting operation of the agency’s science instruments, the science data processors for two of these instruments, and support for the United States members of the international Ocean Surface Topography Science Team.

In August 2014, ISIS swept into Sinjar, a town in northern Iraq and home to many of the country’s Yazidis, a Kurdish-speaking ethnic and religious minority long subjected to persecution. Regarding the Yazidis as infidels, ISIS killed thousands and enslaved thousands of women and girls, in what is now widely recognised as genocide.

The short documentary Into the Fire follows Hana Khider, a Yazidi woman who heads an all-female de-mining team. Khider works for the Mines Advisory Group, one of the founding members of the International Campaign to Ban Landmines, which shared the 1997 Nobel Peace Prize with its coordinator, Jody Williams. The perilous work of Khider’s crew consists of searching for and deactivating hidden explosives left by ISIS, some disguised as everyday objects, including children’s toys. Directed by the British filmmaker Orlando von Einsiedel, the film moves between Khider’s job and her life as a wife and mother, showing two sides of caring for one’s community and rebuilding after the trauma of the genocide.

The film is part of von Einsiedel’s five-part series produced in collaboration with the Nobel Prize and National Geographic, with each instalment focusing on the continuing influence of a different peace laureate.

The mother of slain rapper Drakeo the Ruler has reached a settlement with Live Nation and several other companies over the fatal stabbing of her son backstage at the Once Upon a Time in L.A. music festival in December 2021.

The terms of the settlement were not disclosed in a notice filed with the court, but the agreement was described as conditional, with dismissal contingent on “the satisfactory completion of specified terms to be performed within 45 days.” The language suggests the deal involves obligations that have yet to be fulfilled, potentially including a financial payment. Lawyers for both sides did not respond to requests for comment from Rolling Stone.

Darrylene Corniel, who is the administrator of her son’s estate, sued with claims that her son died “at the hands of a violent mob that was allowed into what should have been a protected and secured area backstage at the music festival.” The other companies involved in her settlement include C3 Presents, Contemporary Services Corporation, Black Tide Events, Bobby Dee Presents, and Hollywood Elite Security.

Drakeo, whose legal name was Darrell Caldwell, was stabbed in the neck by an unidentified assailant shortly before he was scheduled to perform at the festival on Dec. 18, 2021, authorities previously said. He was backstage with his younger brother, Devante Caldwell, a rapper known as Ralfy the Plug, as well as a personal security guard and several members of his Stinc Team music collective.

Corniel previously told Rolling Stone that a crowd surrounded her son around the time that rival rapper YG arrived backstage. About 65 million light-years from Earth, three galaxies don’t look quite right. They aren’t whirlpools bursting with light, but pallid objects dimly illuminated by a smattering of stars. “They have this ghostly appearance,” said Michael Keim, an astrophysicist at Yale University. And this isn’t even the weirdest thing about them.

Dark matter is the invisible glue that keeps the largest structures in the cosmos together. It draws ordinary, visible matter toward it, allowing stars to form and keeping the stelliferous limbs of galaxies from flying off. “Almost all galaxies are dominated by dark matter,” said Shyam Balaji, a theoretical physicist at King’s College London.

But these three diffuse galaxies, known as DF2, DF4, and DF9, have left astronomers stunned. After using a suite of telescopes to estimate their masses — using the motions of their stars as a proxy — the researchers found that all three have little dark matter. Instead, a pittance of ordinary matter alone must have forged their small selection of stars. How could these rule-breaking galaxies have formed?

A paper published in June 2026 in The Astrophysical Journal offers a potential solution. Once upon a time, two regular galaxies collided. Their ordinary matter — their gas and dust — swirled about and got clumped up. But the dark matter passed right through and continued on, like a specter passing through a wall. The cosmic pileup left behind three new galaxies, each bereft of dark matter, each left to struggle to form a new batch of stars.
It’s a convincing explanation for many experts — one that, crucially, may tell us something about the mystery of dark matter.

Some scientists have suggested that dark matter, which has yet to be directly detected, may not exist. Instead, they propose that a tweak to our understanding of the gravitational force might explain various features of the universe.

These bizarre galaxies pour cold water on that idea. “What this is showing is that dark matter is … not just a modification of gravity,” said Keim, who is an author of the new study. If you segregate ordinary matter from dark matter, you’d expect that the dark matter–lacking galaxies would struggle to form stars — and that’s what DF2, DF4, and DF9 show.
That suggests, as many have suspected for some time, that dark matter is a physical thing. “The absence of dark matter is, in a way, some evidence of dark matter, which is ironic,” Balaji said.

What, exactly, is dark matter? Ever since it was formally proposed by the astronomer Fritz Zwicky in the 1930s — and built upon in the 1970s by the astronomer Vera Rubin — cosmologists and astrophysicists have been putting forward their best candidates. Could it be a stealthy type of neutrino? Might it be so-called weakly interacting massive particles, or WIMPs? Some have even opined that it could be primordial black holes as small as individual atoms and as old as the universe itself.

“We don’t know which dark matter candidate is the right one,” said Daniel Whiteson, a particle physicist at the University of California, Irvine. Whatever it is, it has yet to be detected. But “there’s a lot of independent lines of evidence that dark matter is matter.”

Dark matter, which makes up 27% of the universe — and 85% of all matter —interacts with gravity. If it were down to the gravitational pull of ordinary matter alone, stars on the edges of rapidly spinning galaxies would escape into space. Ordinary matter alone would struggle to clump together tightly enough to form stars. Dark matter also seems to warp space itself, bending light around objects in a process known as gravitational lensing.

“You wouldn’t get galaxies without dark matter,” said Chamkaur Ghag, a physicist at University College London. “Is there a way of evolving the galaxies without dark matter in the first place? Our understanding says no.”

So when DF2 was discovered in 2018, astronomers didn’t quite know what to make of it. The galaxy is roughly the same size as the Milky Way, but with 200 times fewer stars, it’s considerably dimmer. Suspicious, scientists used the Keck Observatory in Hawai‘i to track the motions of those stars to estimate its total mass. They discovered that, even for such a star-deficient galaxy, it was lightweight: It seemed to contain, at most, 400 times less dark matter than they would expect, making DF2 the first dark matter–deficient galaxy ever spotted.

In 2019, they observed DF4, another phantom galaxy with a dearth of dark matter. And in 2026, scientists announced that a third, DF9, had joined the club. It contains the mass of roughly 100 million suns, which is consistent with having only ordinary matter. If it were also packed with dark matter, it would be 100 times more massive.
That all three gossamer galaxies existed along a line, as neighbors, didn’t escape the attention of astrophysicists, who began to coalesce around an origin story.

Dark matter is only known to act with the gravitational force; there’s no compelling evidence yet that it interacts with other fundamental forces, like electromagnetism. If two typical galaxies met in a head-on collision, the dark matter would experience very little friction, or drag, and would keep on rocketing by. But ordinary matter, which interacts using all four fundamental forces, would get all tangled up.

“An analogy would be two knights jousting, where the knights and their lances collide and may be thrown to the ground in a heap, while their horses keep on running at full speed,” said Aaron Romanowsky, an astronomer at San José State University.
Several independent experts buy the tale spun by Keim and his colleagues. “It’s very convincing,” Whiteson said.

It’s reminiscent of the Bullet Cluster, two massive collections of galaxies 3.8 billion light-years away that also collided eons ago. This destruction derby, which was recently observed by the James Webb Space Telescope, has a messy distribution of mass that only makes sense if dark matter and ordinary matter got torn asunder during the collision.
Although this kind of segregation can be seen with greater clarity in DF2, DF4, and DF9, not everyone agrees on how the separation took place.

Kinwah Wu, a theoretical astrophysicist at University College London, noted that the triplet does not exhibit any of the fluid, wispy features that one would expect to see after a galactic collision. He suggests that, in this case, DF2, DF4, and DF9 were passing through a large group of massive galaxies. This outsize rabble then stripped the triplet of all their dark matter during their ill-fated voyage.

Stacy McGaugh, an astronomer at Case Western Reserve University and a longtime proponent of modified-gravity theories, is more skeptical. “It’s not clear to me what the formation mechanism is,” he said. An ancient collision “is a plausible origin story, albeit an exceptional one. If that’s what’s happened, then the rest follows.” In other words: If these galaxies were created when their dark matter was stolen away, then it makes sense that dark matter is a physical substance.

“But the question is: Is that what happened?” he continued. “And I’m not convinced that that’s the only way that can happen.” Without definitively knowing their origin story, McGaugh doesn’t think it’s possible to say anything about the nature of dark matter itself.

Most experts, though, cannot see how DF2, DF4, and DF9 could exist without dark matter being a physical thing, even if the trio’s genesis can be debated. “It’s hard to explain how you’d get something like this evolving by itself without something like dark matter,” Ghag said.

That makes this galactic trio bad news for MOND, or modified Newtonian dynamics, an alternative to dark matter proposed in 1983 by the physicist Mordehai Milgrom. “MOND says: What if there’s only visible matter, but its gravity works differently than we thought?” Whiteson explained.

MOND implies that, when objects are experiencing a very weak gravitational pull — for example, when two stars are separated by extreme distances — the gravitational force doesn’t dwindle as much as scientists think. That could explain why spinning galaxies can be held together without needing an extra source of gravity from dark matter, its proponents have argued.

Dark matter has long been the favored theory for cosmologists, as MOND “could never really explain everything,” Ghag said. He explained that MOND suffered a significant blow in 2015 when the U.S.-based Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory, or LIGO, detected gravitational waves — ripples in the fabric of the universe — for the first time. Scientists found that these waves move at the speed of light in all directions over huge distances, which implies that gravity works in a consistent, unmodified way throughout the cosmos.

DF2, DF4, and DF9 are also more elegantly explained by dark matter than by attempts to adjust the mechanics of gravity. “It’s easier to remove matter, cold dark matter, through something like a collision, than it is to turn off a law of nature,” Balaji said.
“I think it’s fine and healthy to have alternative theories and open debate,” Whiteson said. “But let’s also be frank about whether the theory fits the data. MOND does not.”
The identity of dark matter still eludes us. But these galaxies are arguably another nail in the coffin of its increasingly unpopular competitor.
Scientists may have overlooked a hidden Alzheimer's culprit for decades
A long-overlooked peptide once thought harmless could be a hidden contributor to Alzheimer's disease, challenging decades of research and opening new possibilities for treatment.

- For decades, scientists have focused on amyloid beta as a major culprit behind Alzheimerâs disease, spending billions of dollars developing treatments that have often delivered disappointing results. Now, researchers at UC Santa Cruz are drawing attention to a largely overlooked peptide called P3 that could also play a role in the disease. Previously believed to be harmless, P3 can form harmful-looking protein clumps even faster than amyloid beta and may also damage brain cells.

For decades, researchers have invested billions of dollars in Alzheimer's treatments designed to target amyloid beta, a peptide that forms harmful deposits in the brain. But a biochemist at the University of California, Santa Cruz, believes scientists may have overlooked another potential contributor to the disease: a smaller, closely related peptide that was long considered harmless.

In a new commentary published in ChemBioChem, UC Santa Cruz professor Jevgenij Raskatov highlights research suggesting that this lesser-known peptide, called P3, can form microscopic clumps and threadlike structures known as fibrils. Evidence also suggests that P3 may interact with amyloid beta (Aβ), potentially influencing how it accumulates in the brain and how toxic it becomes. These findings raise the possibility that P3 contributes to the nerve cell damage associated with Alzheimer's disease.

"The P3 peptide is, most likely, not the innocent bystander it was commonly thought to be. There's still more research to be done. But this could turn Alzheimer's research on its head," said Raskatov, whose laboratory investigates amyloid peptides in hopes of identifying ways to prevent their harmful effects and develop better Alzheimer's treatments. "P3 is a distinct aggregating peptide that is itself potentially neurotoxic and may be contributing to Alzheimer's disease."
Why Alzheimer's Treatments Have Had Limited Success

Alzheimer's is the most widespread neurodegenerative disease, affecting approximately 35 million people worldwide and generating annual costs exceeding $800 billion. The number of people living with the condition is expected to double by 2050.

Despite decades of intensive research, developing effective treatments has proved extraordinarily difficult. More than 400 clinical trials have investigated potential Alzheimer's drugs, with most focusing on amyloid beta. Many of these efforts have failed, while others have produced only modest benefits. Some treatments have also been associated with serious complications, including brain hemorrhages and strokes.

Amyloid beta originates from a much larger protein embedded in cell membranes called the Amyloid Precursor Protein (APP). Two enzymes, β-secretase and γ-secretase, cut this protein in sequence, releasing amyloid beta peptides of different lengths.

Researchers have concentrated particularly on two versions, Aβ40 and Aβ42, which contain 40 and 42 amino acids, respectively. Aβ42 has attracted the greatest attention because it is especially prone to sticking together and forming toxic aggregates. As a result, it has remained a central target of Alzheimer's drug development for decades.

Existing medications, including cholinesterase inhibitors and N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptor antagonists, can temporarily ease certain symptoms but do not stop the disease from progressing. More recently, antibody treatments such as Lecanemab and Donanemab have been approved to help remove amyloid beta from the brain.
However, Raskatov argues that the benefits achieved so far remain limited, underscoring the need to investigate other biological processes involved in Alzheimer's.
"Progress has been extremely slow, and the current state of the art in Alzheimer's therapy leaves much to be desired," he said. "We need fundamentally new approaches to the problem."
The Overlooked Peptide That May Also Damage Brain Cells

Unlike amyloid beta, P3 forms when Amyloid Precursor Protein is processed through a different sequence of molecular cuts. In this pathway, an enzyme called α-secretase acts first, followed by γ-secretase.
Raskatov has proposed calling this peptide "Amyloid α," or Aα, to better distinguish it from amyloid beta and reflect its ability to form aggregates.

For years, scientists largely assumed that P3 was incapable of forming amyloid deposits, was not toxic to cells, and would remain soluble in water. Under that interpretation, the peptide would simply dissolve rather than accumulate in the brain.

These assumptions were never adequately verified, according to Raskatov. Nevertheless, they helped establish the view that P3 was unlikely to matter in Alzheimer's disease, leaving it largely absent from research efforts.
Raskatov, a specialist in peptide chemistry, and researchers in his laboratory decided to test those long-standing beliefs.

Over the past five years, the team has published three major studies demonstrating that P3 can form amyloid deposits at least as readily as amyloid beta. In fact, their experiments showed that P3 produces these aggregates more rapidly.
The researchers also found evidence that P3 itself may be harmful to neurons, although its toxicity appears lower than that of amyloid beta.

According to Raskatov, an independent research group in the United Kingdom has confirmed and expanded upon his team's findings. Other laboratories are now beginning to investigate how P3 and amyloid beta interact, including whether their relationship affects the accumulation and toxicity of these peptides.

Together, the results challenge the long-held assumption that P3 is biologically harmless and irrelevant to Alzheimer's. However, further research is needed to establish whether and how it contributes to the disease in patients.
Challenging Decades of Alzheimer's Research

For much of the past several decades, amyloid beta has dominated scientific explanations of Alzheimer's disease. David Teplow, an emeritus professor of neurology at UCLA and a prominent Alzheimer's researcher, said the peptide has long been regarded as a central cause of the condition.
But an independent evaluation of Raskatov's research led Teplow to conclude that scientists are beginning to reconsider this narrow focus.

"This reevaluation has far-reaching consequences for both basic science and clinical research into the causes and treatment of Alzheimer's disease," said Teplow, a founding editorial board member of the Journal of Molecular Neuroscience and the American Journal of Neurodegenerative Disease, as well as editor-in-chief of Progress in Molecular Biology and Translational Science.
Raskatov has also encountered a troubling problem while examining how other scientists have interpreted his team's discoveries.

He identified at least four papers published in respected, peer-reviewed journals that cited his laboratory's research as evidence that P3 was harmless and unable to form amyloid deposits. Yet his team's experiments had demonstrated precisely the opposite.
"This is exactly the opposite of what we have actually shown," Raskatov said. "We remain in the dark on how this sort of grand confusion may have come about. Clearly, there is more work ahead of us."

The emerging evidence suggests that understanding Alzheimer's may require looking beyond amyloid beta alone. By examining P3 and its interactions with other amyloid peptides, researchers hope to gain a more complete picture of the processes that damage brain cells and potentially identify new directions for treatment.

That has been the takeaway for officials in GOP groups who have been discussing the state of play with White House aides in recent weeks, according to three sources familiar with the situation.

It all comes as the White House moves into damage-control mode after contemplating for the first time earlier this month, as Inner Loop previously reported, that Republicans could possibly lose both chambers of Congress.
